query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid quenching of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will lead to a significantly enhanced glass-forming ability and improved thermal stability of the amorphous state compared to alloys cooled slowly.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) produced by arc melting that, under slow cooling (~52 K/s), exhibits a mixed or partially crystalline microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply an extreme rapid cooling method (e.g., melt-spinning with cooling rates on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s) immediately after melting.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied while keeping the alloy composition constant, and it is expected to work under controlled processing conditions where only the cooling rate is varied; however, if the cooling rate is too high to the point of introducing detrimental internal stresses, the benefits might be reduced.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased fraction of a homogeneous amorphous phase with suppressed nucleation sites for crystallization.
generation.mechanism: The rapid cooling limits atomic mobility, thereby preventing the rearrangement into a crystalline phase. Phosphorus is thought to disrupt typical bonding networks and enhance the glass-forming ability, thus stabilizing the amorphous structure and delaying crystallization upon heating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a slowly cooled sample, the rapidly quenched alloy will exhibit a higher amorphous phase fraction as confirmed by X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, along with higher onset temperatures for crystallization as revealed by differential scanning calorimetry.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys produced via slower cooling rates resulting in a mixed (predominantly crystalline) microstructure with lower thermal stability.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only within an optimal rapid cooling window; rates insufficient to fully bypass crystallization or so high that they introduce excessive internal stresses might not yield the predicted improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise cooling rate threshold for optimal glass formation and the magnitude of thermal stability enhancement remain to be determined. There is also uncertainty regarding potential adverse effects from internal stresses at extremely high cooling rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy composition. Subject one set to slow cooling (≈52 K/s) and the other set to rapid quenching (using melt-spinning at cooling rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s). Characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, and determine the crystallization onset temperature using differential scanning calorimetry.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to assess phase fraction
Transmission electron microscopy for microstructural analysis
Differential scanning calorimetry to evaluate thermal stability (crystallization onset temperature)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched samples do not show a statistically significant increase in amorphous phase fraction and higher crystallization onset temperatures compared to the slowly cooled samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. Cooling rates significantly influence the microstructure and phase composition of the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy. Slow cooling after arc melting results in a complex microstructure comprising multiple crystalline phases such as FCC “A”, tetragonal “B”, “C”, “D”, and orthorhombic “E”, while faster cooling after a short electric arc pulse reduces the number of phases to primarily FCC “A” and tetragonal “D”. Very rapid cooling using the melt-spinning method results in an amorphous structure, as confirmed by XRD and TEM analyses. Phosphorus addition enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability during rapid cooling. The amorphous structure observed in the melt-spun ribbon demonstrates that the combination of phosphorus and high mixing entropy promotes the formation of amorphous phases during extremely fast cooling. However, further studies are necessary to understand the influence of phosphorus on mechanical properties and limitations, such as reduced ductility.
